transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I’m here because I don’t really know what else to do anymore. I’ve been trying to keep things going, trying to work harder, figure out payment plans, tell myself there’s some way to get the studio back on track, but honestly it feels like none of it is going to matter.

It’s like no matter how much effort I put in, I can’t see things turning around. Not the studio, not my life really. I keep looking at it from every angle, like maybe if I just do this job or take this arrangement or push a little harder, but I don’t believe it anymore. I feel like I’m just standing in front of a wall, and I’m tired of pretending I can build a door through it.
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time lately?

Yeah… most of the time. It’s not just that I get sad here and there, it’s like I wake up and it’s already there before anything has even happened. This heavy, gray kind of feeling, like somebody set a weight on my chest overnight and I’m supposed to just get up and carry it around.

Even when I’m in the shop, which used to be the place where I could sort of lose myself—just the smell of the wood, the tools, figuring out a cut or a joint—it all feels flat now. I’ll be standing there surrounded by things I used to care about, and it’s like there’s no color in it. Sometimes I have to fight not to just stand there staring, because I can’t get myself to feel connected to any of it. So… yeah. Sad, empty, whatever word fits. It’s there most days.
Do you find yourself no longer enjoying activities that you used to find pleasurable?

I don’t know if I’d put it exactly that way. I mean… there are things I used to look forward to, sure, but I haven’t really been stopping to measure whether I’m enjoying them or not. Mostly it all just feels mixed together lately, like I’m going through motions and trying to get through the day.

With the shop, for example, I still care about it in the sense that it matters to me, you know? It’s not like I can just say I don’t care. But whether I’m getting pleasure out of it… I’m not sure. Sometimes I’m so caught up in what needs fixing or what’s not going right that I don’t even know what I’m feeling about the actual work anymore.

So… maybe? I guess I’ve noticed things don’t hit the same way they used to, but I don’t know how much of that is me not enjoying them and how much is just everything feeling heavy right now.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because “lost interest” sounds so clean, like there was a switch and suddenly I didn’t care about things anymore. It doesn’t feel that clear to me.

I guess what I can say is… things don’t pull me toward them the way they used to. Like, with woodworking, I still know it matters to me. I can look at a piece of wood and understand, in my head, why I used to get excited about what it could become. But lately I don’t always feel that spark. Sometimes I’ll start something and I’m more aware of the effort than anything else—what has to be done, what might go wrong, what I’m behind on—so it’s hard to tell if I’m uninterested or just worn down.

So… maybe I have, some. But I don’t know that I’d say I’ve completely lost interest. It’s more like the interest is buried under a lot of noise, and I can’t always reach it.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

I don’t think so… not anything I’d call significant. I mean, I don’t really weigh myself regularly, so I might not be the best judge. My clothes seem to fit about the same, I guess. Maybe some days I feel like I look a little different, but that might just be how I’m seeing myself in the mirror more than an actual change.

So, no… I haven’t noticed a big weight change recently.
Do you feel like you've been moving more slowly than usual or having trouble sitting still?

I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself, like, pacing around or being unable to sit still in a way that stands out. And I don’t think I’ve been obviously moving slower either, at least not that anyone’s pointed out to me.

I mean, some days I probably take longer to get going, but I don’t know if that’s the kind of thing you mean. With work, I’m still moving around because I have to, and when I’m sitting, I’m usually just sitting there. I don’t feel especially restless, like I need to jump up every few minutes.

So… I guess no, not in any clear way. If it’s happening, I haven’t really been aware of it.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened?

Yeah… I do. Probably more than I should, if I’m being honest.

It’s not always about some big thing that happened, though. A lot of the time it’s work stuff, and I know work mistakes happen, I know that. Like if a joint doesn’t line up perfectly, or I cut something a little off and have to redo it, or I miss getting a bid in on time… in my head I don’t just go, “Okay, that was a mistake, fix it and move on.” I go straight to, “What is wrong with me?” or “Maybe I’m not actually that good at this.” And then it turns into this bigger thing, like I’m a lousy carpenter, or I had no business trying to run my own studio in the first place.

And I can usually see, at least later, that that’s a pretty harsh jump. I mean, one bad joint doesn’t mean the whole house falls down, you know? But in the moment it doesn’t feel like one mistake. It feels like proof. Like I’ve been pretending I can handle things and the mistake is just showing what’s really true.

So yes, I blame myself a lot. Even for things that are probably just normal problems. I have a hard time keeping them normal in my own mind.
How long have you been feeling this heavy, gray feeling that you described?

It’s been… a little over two years now. I’d put it at about two years and maybe two months.

It started around when I took on the mortgage for the studio. I remember that pretty clearly because that was kind of the point where everything started feeling heavier. Not all at once, exactly, but from around then, that gray feeling just sort of settled in and never really lifted for long.

So yeah… about two years and two months, give or take.
Have you had any periods in the last two years where you felt significantly better for at least a couple of months?

No… not really. I mean, there have been days here and there where I wasn’t quite as weighed down, or maybe I was distracted enough by work that I didn’t sit with it as much, but I wouldn’t say there’s been a stretch of a couple months where I felt significantly better.

It’s been pretty steady since I took on the studio mortgage, a little over two years ago. About two years and two months now, I guess. That was when it kind of settled in, and since then it hasn’t really lifted in any lasting way. Like, it might ease up for a day or a weekend, but not for months.
Can you think of anything recently that you've done and actually enjoyed, where you felt some pleasure or happiness?

Honestly… I’m trying to think of something, and that’s kind of the problem. There are things I do that I know I used to enjoy. Being in the shop, for example. I mean, wood used to be the thing that could pull me in — the smell of it, picking through boards, seeing the grain, figuring out how a piece was going to come together. That used to give me something. Not always excitement exactly, but satisfaction. A little spark, I guess.

Lately, though, most days I wake up and it’s like that heavy gray feeling is already sitting on me before I’ve even done anything. And then I get to the shop, and I’m surrounded by all the stuff I used to love, and it just feels… flat. Like I’m looking at it through dirty glass or something. I’ll stand there with a board in front of me, tools right there, and instead of feeling interested or proud or even calm, I have to fight not to just stand there staring.

So, recently? I don’t know. Maybe there are moments where something is less bad, or I get through a task and feel a little relief that it’s done. But actual pleasure or happiness… I’m having a hard time coming up with that.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or wishing you could just disappear?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly.

I mean, I don’t sit there with some clear plan in my head, if that’s what you’re asking. But there are times where I just feel so tired of being in my own life that the idea of not having to wake up and do it all again… it crosses my mind. Not in a dramatic way, more like this quiet thought of, “What if I could just not be here for a while?” Or disappear somewhere nobody needed anything from me.

It’s hard to say out loud because part of me feels like if I say it, it sounds worse than how I mean it. But yes, I guess I have had thoughts like wishing I could just vanish, or go to sleep and not have to deal with everything. I don’t know if that’s the same as not wanting to live exactly, but it’s… close enough that I probably shouldn’t pretend it isn’t there.
Can you think of any activity, no matter how small, that you have looked forward to in the past few weeks?

I wish I had a better answer, but… not really. I keep trying to think of something small, because I know it doesn’t have to be some big enjoyable thing, but even the small stuff feels kind of blank lately.

Like, normally the shop would be the obvious answer. There used to be mornings where I’d at least look forward to getting my hands on a piece of wood, or seeing how the grain came out after a cut, or just having that quiet stretch where it was me and the tools and the work. But most days now I wake up and that heavy, gray feeling is already there before I’ve even started the day. By the time I get to the shop, I’m surrounded by all the things that used to mean something to me, and it just feels flat. I’ll stand there looking at wood I know I should care about, and I have to push myself just to move instead of staring at it.

So in the past few weeks… I can’t really say I’ve looked forward to much. Maybe I’ve looked forward to being done with something, or to getting through the day, but that’s not the same as looking forward to an activity. It’s more like waiting for things to be over.
Can you recall any recent situation where you felt a sense of pleasure or enjoyment, no matter how small it might seem?

I know I keep circling back to the same answer, but… no, not really. I’m trying to be fair about it, because maybe there was some tiny second where something felt okay and I’m just not giving it credit, but nothing stands out as pleasure.

Most days I wake up and that heavy, gray feeling is already there, like it got up before I did and was waiting. And then I’ll go into the shop, where you’d think if anything was going to help, it would be that. I mean, I’m surrounded by wood and tools and the kind of work that used to hold my attention. I used to be able to lose myself in it a little.

But lately it all just feels flat. I’ll be standing there with a board in front of me, and I know I used to care about the grain or the cut or how the piece would come together, but I don’t feel it. It’s like I’m going through the motions, and sometimes I have to fight just to not stand there staring at it. So if there’s enjoyment, it’s so small I can’t really catch it. It’s more like I get through something, not that I enjoy it.
Can you remember the last time you felt genuine pleasure or interest in something?

Honestly… I’m having a hard time remembering one. I keep trying to go back through the last stretch of days or weeks and find something I can point to, like, “There, that was it,” but it all kind of has the same color to it, if that makes sense.

Most days I wake up and it’s like this heavy, gray feeling is already sitting on me before I’ve even done anything. I don’t wake up neutral and then get dragged down by the day — it’s already there. And that makes it hard to tell when the last real pleasure was, because even things that used to get through to me don’t really seem to anymore.

The shop used to be that place for me. I mean, working with wood wasn’t just a job in my head. There were parts of it I genuinely cared about — the smell of it, the feel of a good board, seeing the grain come out, figuring out how a piece was going to fit together. I used to get interested without even trying. But now I can be standing right there, surrounded by all of it, and it just feels flat. Like I know I’m supposed to care, and I remember caring, but I can’t reach it.

Sometimes I’ll just stand there looking at the wood or the tools, and I have to force myself to move, because otherwise I could just stay there staring. Not because I’m thinking deeply about it or enjoying it — more because nothing in me is catching on it. So… the honest answer is I don’t really remember the last time I felt genuine pleasure or interest. I remember what it used to feel like, but I don’t remember the last time I actually felt it.
Can you think of any recent activity that you found pleasurable or enjoyable?

Not really, no. I know I probably sound like I’m repeating myself, but I keep looking for something I can honestly say was enjoyable, and I just… I can’t find much.

Even the shop, which used to be the thing I could count on, doesn’t really do it lately. I’ll be in there surrounded by the wood and tools, things I used to care about without even thinking, and it all feels kind of flat. Like I know, in my head, that I used to love the work — choosing a piece, seeing the grain, getting into the rhythm of it — but lately I’m just standing there with this heavy gray feeling already on me from the minute I wake up.

Sometimes I’ll look at a board or a half-finished piece and I have to make myself move, because otherwise I could just stand there staring at it. Not enjoying it, not really thinking anything useful, just… stuck. So if you’re asking about something pleasurable or enjoyable recently, I don’t think I can honestly say there’s been one. At most I get through things. I don’t really enjoy them.
Have you noticed a lack of pleasure in activities that normally would bring you happiness?

Yes. Very much so. I mean, that’s probably one of the things that bothers me the most, because it’s not like I’m just bored with something new or tired of a hobby I picked up last week. It’s the things that used to feel like mine, especially the shop.

Most days I wake up and that heavy, gray feeling is already there, like it’s sitting on my chest before I’ve even had a chance to do anything. And then I go into the shop, and I’m surrounded by wood and tools and pieces I know I used to care about. I used to notice the grain, the smell, the way a board would feel in my hands, all of that. It used to bring me something — maybe not happiness in some big dramatic way, but satisfaction, interest, a reason to keep going with it.

Now it just feels flat. I can look at the same kind of wood I used to get excited about and there’s just nothing there. Sometimes I have to actually fight not to just stand there staring at it, because I’m not drawn into it the way I used to be. It’s like I remember that it used to matter to me, but I can’t feel that anymore. So yes, I’ve definitely noticed a lack of pleasure. It’s pretty hard to miss.
Do you feel like your current state is interfering with your ability to function in daily life?

Yes. Yeah, it is. I wish I could say it was just making things feel harder, but I’m past that. It’s starting to affect the actual nuts and bolts of my life.

With the studio, I’m not keeping up the way I used to. I’ve missed bids — jobs I should have followed up on, people who were waiting to hear from me, and I just didn’t get it together in time. And some of those were clients who used to call me first, you know? People I had a relationship with, people who trusted me. Now I can feel that slipping because I’m not returning calls quickly enough or I’m not getting estimates out, and then they go somewhere else. I don’t really blame them. I just… I can see it happening and still can’t seem to keep up.

And it’s not only the woodworking part. It’s all the basic running-the-business stuff. Paperwork, scheduling, bills, the kind of things that were never fun but I could at least manage. I’ve let mortgage paperwork pile up, and every time I see the stack I tell myself I’m going to sit down and handle it, and then it just sits there another day. Then another. It starts to feel bigger than it probably is, but I still don’t do it.

I’ve also pulled back from people and places that used to matter to me. I stopped going to gallery openings, even ones where I know people and should probably show my face. And pickup basketball, too — I used to go, not even because I was great at it, but because it got me around people and out of my own head for a while. Now I just don’t go.

So, yes, it’s interfering. I’m barely keeping a foothold in the work and the people that used to make up my life.
Have your symptoms been continuous or have you had periods where you felt completely back to normal?

It’s been pretty continuous, yeah. I don’t really feel like I’ve had a stretch where I was completely back to normal.

If I’m trying to put a time on it, it really started around when I took on the studio mortgage. That was a little over two years ago now — about two years and two months, I guess. I remember because the mortgage was such a big turning point in my head, like this line where everything was supposed to become more solid and legitimate, and instead that’s about when this heaviness started settling in.

There may have been days here and there that were less bad, where I got through more or didn’t feel quite as buried, but I wouldn’t call that normal. Not like I was myself again. It’s more like the volume changes a little, but it doesn’t really go away.
Can you think of any activity that you used to enjoy, but now you don't find pleasure in it anymore?

The shop, definitely. That’s the clearest one.

I mean, I used to really enjoy being in there. Not every single part of it, obviously — some of it is work — but there was something about the wood itself that used to pull me in. I’d notice the grain, the weight of a board, the smell when I cut into it. I could get interested in a piece before I even knew exactly what I was going to make from it.

Now most days I wake up and there’s already this heavy, gray feeling sitting on me, and by the time I’m in the shop, it’s like everything is muted. I’m surrounded by the same tools and the same wood I used to love, but it just feels flat. Sometimes I’ll be standing there looking at a board, and I have to fight not to just stand there staring at it, because there’s no spark there anymore. I remember that I used to care about it, but I don’t really feel the pleasure in it now.
Have your symptoms been present for the majority of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Yes… I mean, if you’re asking whether it’s been most of the day and almost every day, then yes. It hasn’t just been a bad week or a stretch where I was in a slump.

This has been going on since I took on the studio mortgage, a little over two years ago now — about two years and two months, give or take. That’s the marker I keep coming back to, because that’s when I remember it really settling in and not lifting. It’s been there most days since then.

doctor.intent: determine presence of guilt or self-blame
doctor.question: Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened?

target_item.name: Low_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: When a joint doesn't line up perfect or I miss a bid deadline, I don't just think I made a mistake—I start thinking I'm a lousy carpenter and maybe I had no business trying to run my own studio.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about guilt and self-blame, which most directly aligns with the profile describing chronic negative self-evaluation and blaming oneself for mistakes.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I do. Probably more than I should, if I’m being honest.

It’s not always about some big thing that happened, though. A lot of the time it’s work stuff, and I know work mistakes happen, I know that. Like if a joint doesn’t line up perfectly, or I cut something a little off and have to redo it, or I miss getting a bid in on time… in my head I don’t just go, “Okay, that was a mistake, fix it and move on.” I go straight to, “What is wrong with me?” or “Maybe I’m not actually that good at this.” And then it turns into this bigger thing, like I’m a lousy carpenter, or I had no business trying to run my own studio in the first place.

And I can usually see, at least later, that that’s a pretty harsh jump. I mean, one bad joint doesn’t mean the whole house falls down, you know? But in the moment it doesn’t feel like one mistake. It feels like proof. Like I’ve been pretending I can handle things and the mistake is just showing what’s really true.

So yes, I blame myself a lot. Even for things that are probably just normal problems. I have a hard time keeping them normal in my own mind.
